en: Preface to the Commentary on the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra:

From the time of the Fifth Patriarch onward, he began to exhort both monastics and laypeople to recite the *Vajracchedikā*. He maintained that by merely reciting this sūtra, one can realize one's own nature (*svabhāva*).
He attained Buddhahood, and thus the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* became highly esteemed by the world.
I have repeatedly recited this sūtra three times and have privately concluded that its great purport lies in the Buddha’s instruction to Subhūti: "One should abide thus and thus subdue the mind."
To abide is to abide in this mind; to subdue is to subdue this mind.
Both are precisely what is called the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* mind; there are not two minds. To abide is substantiality; to subdue is emptiness.
To abide thus is itself to subdue. Therefore, there is neither reality nor unreality; this is the great purport of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
To illustrate this through Confucian principles: Zengzi asked, "Is there one word by which one may practice throughout one's entire life?
The Master said, "It is 'reciprocity' (*shu*). What you do not wish done to yourself, do not do to others. This is what is meant by "abiding in this manner. Master...
Gong said, "I do not wish others to impose [their will] upon me, and I likewise wish not to impose [my will] upon others.
The Master said, "Ci, this is beyond your reach. It is what is meant by 'subduing [the mind] in this manner.

The Master said, "He who wears a tattered inner robe of coarse wool and stands alongside those wearing fox-fur and raccoon-dog fur without feeling ashamed—is it not Ryou? He is neither vindictive nor covetous. What..."
"Using it is not good. This refers to what is called "dwelling thus. Zilu recited this for the rest of his life.
The Master said, "How can this way alone be sufficient to be 'good'? This refers to what is called "subduing thus. Not dwelling is certainly not [dwelling];

this is what is meant by "subduing while not subduing. Furthermore, how could one dwell? Within the sutra, the phrase "it is precisely not... appears several times as a name and phrase. It is precisely... [as follows].

"Non-being" refers to subduing; "being" refers to abiding. Those who interpret this sutra according to worldly conventions claim that one should abide in the true mind and subdue the deluded mind, thereby dividing them into two. This fails to grasp the meaning of the entire sutra.
Indeed, during the Hongwu era, the monk Zongle, having received an imperial decree to annotate the sutra, explained it in this same manner. Thus, it is said:
The meaning of this sutra has long been obscured. This scripture expounds the principle that abiding is itself subduing;
reaching the point where no dharma can be apprehended and no dharma can be spoken is the truly unsurpassed and profoundly deep, wondrous meaning.
Yet, fearing its dissemination within the Middle Kingdom might cause people to treat the Buddha-dharma with contempt, the disciples of the Buddha subsequently made arbitrary additions to it.
It is often said that those who receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra possess immeasurable and boundless merit.
While this reflects the sincere hardship of protecting the Dharma, if one causes the text to be fragmented and its meaning to remain obscure, one cannot escape blame.

For instance, the statement, "All worthy and holy ones are distinguished by means of the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*)," serves as the basis for the following discussion concerning the *srotāpanna*.
The various passages concerning the *srotāpanna* begin from the stage of the *srotāpanna* up to that of the Tathāgata; these are what are known as "all the worthy and holy ones.
Yet, suddenly in the midst of this, there is inserted a passage regarding the giving of the seven treasures, which renders the textual meaning disjointed.
This is the first proof that later generations interpolated [the text]. Furthermore, when the Buddha says, "That which is not a body is called the Great Body," this is a metaphor.
This is an illustrative expression. The passage below, where the Buddha says that "prajñāpāramitā is indeed not prajñāpāramitā," constitutes the primary meaning.
However, if the text were to insert the section on the giving of the seven treasures in between, the coherence of the textual meaning would be severed.
This is the second proof that later generations added [these passages]. For instance, when the Buddha has finished speaking a sutra, he often concludes with words of praise;

as it says at the end of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: "If there are sentient beings who can recite this sutra and uphold this mantra, they will directly attain Bodhi, and no further demonic activities shall arise. This is indeed a standard convention. Yet, in this [present] sutra, [such praise] occurs everywhere.

The scriptural text had not yet reached its midpoint, and the Buddha’s intent had not yet been proclaimed, when Subhūti suddenly asked whether sentient beings would believe it, and the World-Honored One suddenly began to extol the merit of this sutra.
How could they have been so hasty? This is evidence that later generations added these passages.
Third: When the text of a sutra has concluded, it traditionally indicates the title of the sutra itself. For example, at the end of the *Mahāsthāmaprāpta-gṛhapati-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, it says:
Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying, "By what name should this sutra be called? How should we receive and uphold it?
The Buddha told Ānanda, "This sutra is named the *Mahāyāna-sūtra Asked by the Householder Mahāsthāmaprāpta*. This is also a standard convention; thus, this [is the case here].
In the so-called thirteenth division of the *Sūtra*, [the passage] is extracted directly from it; yet, before stating the actual text of the sūtra, the title of the sūtra is mentioned first.
Thus, both Subhūti’s question and the World-Honored One’s answer are misplaced. This is the fourth proof that later generations have interpolated [the text].
Furthermore, the "four-line verse" is mentioned repeatedly, but it is unclear what is being referred to. Some take it to mean, for instance, if...
The four lines regarding "seeing me by means of form," or alternatively, the four lines regarding "all conditioned phenomena" (saṃskṛtadharma), both appear later in the text.
At the time when the Buddha spoke these four-line verses, these specific four-line verses did not yet exist.
How could Subhūti have failed to ask what these four lines were? Having read the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, I know that which is called the "four-line verse."
Being free from identity, difference, both, or neither; existence, non-existence, both, or neither;
permanence, or impermanence—this accords quite well with the purport of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Yet, these are not actually words found within the *Vajracchedikā* itself.

It is suspected that the Buddha frequently used these four phrases alongside the *Vajracchedikā* when instructing his disciples during his lifetime, and later generations subsequently associated them with it. This...

This is the fifth proof that later generations have added interpolations. Given these five proofs, we know that the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* indeed contains words appended by later people.
Just as weeds mixed with grain cause the essence of the crop to become increasingly obscured, so too has this sutra originally lacked chapter divisions;
yet it is now divided into thirty-two sections, claiming these were established by Prince Zhaoming of the Liang Dynasty. Whether this is true remains unknown. I do not accept it.
The various mental divisions and their falsely established designations are not, in reality, the root of goodness; they are insufficient to be relied upon.

I, a humble scholar of mere words and phrases, now in the twilight of my life, have turned to the study of Buddhism out of necessity. While I certainly have heard nothing of the great meaning of the [Buddha’s] Western arrival, I have privately attained a unique insight into this sutra.
Disregarding my own meager learning, I have composed these annotations, dividing them into two parts: the first and the second.
There are two chapters: the upper chapter contains seven sections and the lower chapter contains eleven sections, totaling eighteen sections.

Regarding the supplementary passages that have been handed down for a long time and were likewise transmitted from the Western lands, I have not dared to delete them; instead, I have set them apart in a separate line below the main text.
If scholars wish to recite and study the full text, it is complete herein. However, if they wish to investigate its underlying purport, then...

Having eliminated the superfluous and the weeds, the True Scripture reveals itself. Although it may appear to contain repetitions from beginning to end, its underlying structure is, in fact, clearly defined.
One can thus grasp the general essence of what the Fifth Patriarch meant when he said that by merely reciting this scripture, one can realize one's nature and attain Buddhahood.
Written by the Layman of Qu Yuan, Yu Yue, on a boat in Wujiang in the tenth month of the ninth year of the Guangxu era.
*The Diamond Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Upper Section;
annotated by the Layman of Qu Yuan, Yu Yue.
Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
Then, at the time for eating, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took his bowl, and entered the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food.
Having gone through the city in order, begging from house to house, he returned to his original location and ate his meal.
[The meal] was finished. Having gathered his robe and bowl and washed his feet, he spread out a seat and sat down.

At that time, the Elder Subhūti, rising from his seat amidst the great assembly, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is rare, World-Honored One! The Tathāgata well protects and sustains all bodhisattvas; he well entrusts all bodhisattvas. World-Honored One...
“World-Honored One, how should a son or daughter of good family who has resolved upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* abide?
How can they subdue their minds? How can they bring them to emptiness? The Buddha said, “Excellent, excellent, Subhūti!
It is as you have said. The Tathāgata well protects and sustains all bodhisattvas; he well entrusts all bodhisattvas to you.”

"Now listen attentively; I shall explain it for you. Sons and daughters of good family who have resolved their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should abide in this way and thus subdue their minds. "So be it, World-Honored One;
we wish to hear it with joy. (The first section ends here.)

Subhūti asked: "How should one abide? How should one subdue the mind? This mind is precisely what was referred to in the preceding text as the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi-citta* (the mind of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment). To "abide" means to abide in this mind;
to "subdue" means to subdue this mind. There are not two minds. If one can abide [in it], then one can possess [it].
If one can subdue [the mind], then one can be without it. This is the great purport of this sutra.
The conventional interpretation—which claims that one dwells peacefully in the true mind while subduing the deluded mind—divides them into two and completely misses its essential meaning.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should subdue their minds in this way—(the word 'abide' is not mentioned for the sake of brevity)—regarding all categories of sentient beings:
those born from eggs, those born from wombs, those born from moisture, or those born by transformation;
those with form or without form; those with perception, those without perception, or those who are neither with nor without perception."
"I shall cause them all to enter *nirvāṇa* without remainder and bring them to final liberation. In this way, I liberate immeasurable, incalculable, and boundless sentient beings.

(This is what is meant by "one should abide thus. "In reality, there is not a single sentient being who has attained liberation. (This is what is meant by "one should subdue the mind thus. Why is this?
Subhūti, if a bodhisattva possesses the notion of a self, the notion of a person, the notion of a sentient being, or the notion of a life-span...
[Characteristics]. This is not a bodhisattva (the second section on the right).
The traditional interpretation claims that in this section the Buddha first addressed Subhūti, saying, "One should subdue [the mind] in this manner," but this is incorrect.
The subsequent chapter states: "At that time, Subhūti said to the Buddha: 'World-Honored One, good sons and good daughters...'"
When a woman sets her mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, how should she abide?

How should she subdue her mind? The Buddha told Subhūti: "A son of good family or a daughter of good family who has set their mind upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should give rise to this thought: 'I should extinguish [the afflictions]...'"
"To deliver all sentient beings; having delivered all sentient beings, yet there is not a single sentient being who has been truly delivered," and so forth.
Although this passage is cited specifically [to illustrate] "abiding" and "subduing," it does not distinguish between them.
Therefore, this passage must also not be speaking with distinction. As the Sūtra says:
"One should subdue the mind in this manner. It does not say "one should abide in this manner," for the text is simply incomplete.
This is based on the version by Kumārajīva; the other versions differ from the above in their wording.
These include the version by Bodhiruci of the Wei dynasty, the versions by Paramārtha of the Chen dynasty and Xuanzang of the Great Tang, and the version by Yijing of the Tang dynasty.
In both versions, the four characters "how to practice" (云何修行) appear. Therefore, commentators take "abiding," "cultivating," and "subduing" as the three meanings.
However, following the phrase "wishing with longing to hear," the Buddha does not repeat the preceding text;

this shows that the Buddha’s words were intended to clarify the great meaning rather than to provide a detailed, itemized analysis from the outset. In Kumārajīva’s version, there is indeed the word "should" (應).
The single phrase "thus subduing the mind" causes the Buddha’s words to appear as if they were biased or attached to something.
For the sake of brevity, I have provisionally included it; however, in reality, these seven characters are merely redundant.

This can be known by verifying it against the subsequent section, where their absence becomes clear. It can also be known by verifying it against various editions, where they likewise do not exist. Therefore...
Thus, abiding is itself subduing; fundamentally there are not two states. From where, then, could one speak of distinguishing between them?
This dharma of abiding and subduing is nothing other than non-self (*anātman*). Therefore it is said:
"One who thoroughly penetrates the dharma of non-self is truly a Bodhisattva. Where there is self, there is person; where there is self and person...
Among humans, there are both the beautiful and the ugly; thus, [the text] uses "self," "person," "multitude," and "life" to encompass these.

The marks of sentient beings and the marks of life are merely expressions for the marks of the ugly and the marks of the beautiful. The liberation of sentient beings is not what is emphasized in the ultimate meaning;
it is used merely as a provisional expression. It is like the words of Confucius in the *Analects*: "My aspiration is that the elderly shall be at peace, my friends shall trust me, and the young..."
To "cherish it" is likewise to borrow these terms for the sake of discourse. For the mind is fundamentally empty and void; it manifests through phenomena.
Thus, what is here called "nirvāṇa" (extinction) and what is said below regarding "generosity" have the same meaning.
From the passage "whether born from eggs or born from wombs" onwards, this is merely an extensive exposition. Sentient beings perceive them as immeasurable, innumerable, and boundless. At first...
There is no profound meaning here; yet those who interpret it claim that the womb-born, egg-born, moisture-born, and transformation-born are all metaphors for the mind.
These are but fragmented words and convoluted explanations—seeking depth, they instead fall into superficiality.
Furthermore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva should practice giving without dwelling on anything at all regarding phenomena.
That is to say, they should not dwell on form when practicing giving; they should not dwell on sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena when practicing giving.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva should give in this manner: without dwelling on signs.
Why is this? If a bodhisattva practices giving without dwelling on signs, that merit is inconceivable and immeasurable.
Subhūti, what do you think? Can the empty space in the eastern direction be measured? "No, World-Honored One.
Subhūti, can the empty space in the south, west, north, the four intermediate directions, and above and below be measured? "No, World-Honored One."
"Venerable Subhūti, it is the same with the merit of a bodhisattva who practices giving without dwelling on signs; it is likewise inconceivable.
Subhūti, a bodhisattva should simply dwell as thus instructed. (The third section, right).
Subhūti asked, "How should one dwell? To which the Buddha replied that one should dwell in non-dwelling;
for if the mind dwells anywhere, it is not dwelling at all. Thus, non-dwelling is itself dwelling, and this very dwelling is subduing.
The preceding passage spoke in terms of parinirvāṇa, having already clarified the Bodhisattva’s absence of self, person, multitude, or life-span.
"Characteristics. This is spoken again in terms of giving, and it concludes by saying, "one should not dwell in characteristics.
Not dwelling in characteristics is precisely because there are no characteristics. All of this was told by the Buddha to Subhūti;
it is the essential meaning of "dwelling" and "subduing" simultaneously. Therefore, it is said: "A bodhisattva should simply dwell as instructed. If one does not act accordingly...
Regarding the instruction on "abiding," this would constitute the greed and attachment of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
According to the traditional interpretation, the preceding section is the Buddha’s teaching to Subhūti that one should subdue [the mind] in this manner;

this present section is the Buddha’s teaching to Subhūti that one should abide in the fruit of Buddhahood in this manner. If explained analytically, these should follow the sequence of the questions asked.
"Why does one first subdue [the mind] and only afterwards abide [in it]?
Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of physical marks? No, World-Honored One;
the Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of physical marks. Why is this? The physical marks spoken of by the Tathāgata are not, in fact, physical marks."
[On] Marks. (Form is emptiness. The Buddha told Subhūti: "Whatever marks there are, all are false and illusory. If one perceives that all marks are no-marks, then one sees the Tathāgata."

Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, will there be any sentient beings who, upon hearing such spoken words and phrases, will give rise to true faith? The Buddha told Subhūti, "Do not speak thus.

After the Tathāgata has passed into extinction, during the final five hundred years, there will be those who uphold the precepts and cultivate merit who will be able to give rise to faith in these words and phrases."
Subhūti, you should know that such a person has not planted roots of goodness under one, two, three, four, or five Buddhas;
rather, they have already planted various roots of goodness under immeasurable thousands, tens of thousands, and millions of Buddhas.
Subhūti, when these beings hear these phrases and give rise to pure faith for even a single thought-moment, the Tathāgata knows them all and sees them all.
One attains such immeasurable merit. Why is this?
These sentient beings no longer possess the mark of a self, the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, or the mark of a life-span.
They possess no mark of dharmas, nor do they possess any mark of non-dharmas (which refers to what was said above: that all marks are non-marks). Why is this? Because these sentient beings...
[Arising. (The four characters are redundant. If the mind grasps at signs, one is attached to the notions of self, person, sentient being, and life-span. (All signs whatsoever arise from the mind.

If one grasps at the sign of dharmas, one is likewise attached to the notions of self, person, sentient being, and life-span. (This is to cling to existence as inherently real. Why is this? (The three characters are redundant.

If one grasps at the sign of non-dharmas, one is likewise attached to the notions of self, person, sentient being, and life-span. (To cling to non-existence is also a form of attachment. Therefore, one should not...
Take up the Dharma; you should not take up what is not the Dharma. For this reason, the Tathāgata has constantly said:
"O bhikṣus, understand my teaching of the Dharma as being like the parable of the raft. Even the Dharma should be relinquished, let alone what is not the Dharma. (This concludes the fourth section.)

This cause does not abide in signs; to speak of it in its ultimate sense, even the characteristics of phenomena and the non-characteristics of phenomena must both not exist, and even "phenomena" itself must not exist. Therefore, it concludes with the statement that even the Dharma should be relinquished.
The Dharma should be abided in thus; relinquishment should be subdued thus.
Subhūti, what do you think? Has the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?

"Has the Tathāgata preached any Dharma? Subhūti replied, "As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has taught, there is no fixed dharma called 'anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,' nor is there any fixed dharma that the Tathāgata can preach."

"If one abides, then it is fixed; yet as soon as one abides, one subdues [the mind], and thus there is no fixedness. Why is this? All dharmas taught by the Tathāgata are ungraspable, because there is no fixed dharma.
They are ineffable, because there is nothing to be attained. They are not dharmas, because they lack substantiality; they are not non-dharmas, because they lack unreality. Why is this so?

Because all worthies and sages are distinguished by means of the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). (The phrase "all worthies and sages" includes those from the stage of *srotāpanna* upward, as mentioned in the following text. From the first fruit, the *srotāpanna*...

From the stage of Stream-enterer up to the attainment of Buddhahood, they are all identical in that they are distinguished by means of the unconditioned dharma (as will be explained in detail in the following passage).

Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to fill a trichiliocosm with the seven treasures and give them as a gift, would the merit obtained by that person be great? Subhūti replied, "It would be very great."
"World-Honored One, why is this? It is because that merit is not a substantial nature of merit; therefore, the Tathāgata says the merit is great.

Furthermore, if there is someone who, from within this sutra, receives and maintains even as little as a four-line verse and explains it to others, their virtue surpasses the former. Why is this? Subhūti, all Buddhas and..."
The Buddha’s Dharma of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* all issues from this sutra.
Subhūti, that which is called the "Buddha-Dharma" is not, in fact, Buddha-Dharma. (From the *srotāpanna* up to the Buddha, all are the Buddha-Dharma; yet all are not the Buddha-Dharma.
The Buddha spoke this to inspire Subhūti and to introduce the following passage. Subhūti, what do you think? Can a *srotāpanna* [form such a thought]?
[The Buddha] asked, "Do you think that I have attained the fruit of a Srotāpanna? Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is this? The name 'Srotāpanna' means 'one who has entered the stream.
(A Srotāpanna should abide in this way. Yet there is nothing entered; they do not enter form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas.

(A Srotāpanna should subdue [the mind] in this way. This is called a Srotāpanna. That which is called the dharma of a Srotāpanna is not, in fact, a dharma of a Srotāpanna. (The following section concerns the Sakṛdāgāmin.)
[He is] an Anāgāmin. [This is] stated in general terms; it is not explained in detail. Subhūti, what do you think?
Does a Sakṛdāgāmin have the thought, "I have attained the fruit of a Sakṛdāgāmin"? Subhūti said, "No, World-Honored One. Why is this?
A Sakṛdāgāmin is so named because he returns once more, yet in reality there is no coming and going. It is for this reason that he is called a Sakṛdāgāmin. Subhūti, at...
"What do you think? Does a *anāgāmin* have this thought: 'I have attained the fruit of *anāgāmin*'?
Subhūti replied: 'No, World-Honored One. Why is that? One is called an *anāgāmin* because they do not return; yet in reality, there is no such thing as "not returning."'"
"This is called an Anāgāmin. Subhūti, what do you think? Does an Arhat have this thought: 'I have attained the path of Arhatship'?
Subhūti replied, "No, World-Honored One. Why is that? Because there is truly no dharma named 'Arhat'.
(This completes the preceding section: since there is truly no dharma named 'Arhat,' then likewise there is truly no dharma named 'Srotāpanna,' 'Sakṛdāgāmin,' or 'Anāgāmin'—all are without self.)

"World-Honored One, if an Arhat were to have this thought: 'I have attained the path of Arhatship,' he would immediately be attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span (and the same applies to those from Anāgāmin downwards).

World-Honored One, the Buddha has said that I am foremost among men in the attainment of the Samādhi of Non-Contention, and that I am an Arhat who is foremost in being free from desire; yet I do not harbor such a thought as: 'I am...'"

“World-Honored One, I am an Arhat free from desire. World-Honored One, if I were to have the thought, ‘I have attained the path of Arhatship,’ then the World-Honored One would not say that Subhūti is one who delights in the practice of araṇā. This is because Subhūti has, in reality, no practice at all;
it is for this reason that Subhūti is said to delight in the practice of araṇā. (This is Subhūti’s own clarification of the meaning of the dharma of non-action. The Buddha [said]:
The Buddha addressed Subhūti: "What do you think? Did the Tathāgata, when he was formerly with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, obtain anything regarding the Dharma?
"No, World-Honored One. When the Tathāgata was with the Buddha Dīpaṃkara, he truly obtained nothing regarding the Dharma.

(Here again, the Buddha himself, by means of his own intention, inspires Subhūti to clarify the meaning of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) Dharma. For although there are distinctions from the stage of Srotāpanna up to that of the Buddha, they are all one and the same in terms of the unconditioned Dharma. Subhūti...
"Subhūti, what do you think? Does a bodhisattva adorn buddha-fields? "No, World-Honored One. Why is this?
That which is called 'adorning a buddha-field' is not actually adorning; it is merely named 'adornment. (If one knows that non-adornment is true adornment, that is indeed true adornment.
This statement is made to introduce the meaning of purity in the following passage. Therefore, Subhūti, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should thus give rise to purity."

Purifying the mind. (That which is pure is the exhaustion of all things. One should not give rise to the mind by dwelling on forms. One should not give rise to the mind by dwelling on sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas.
One should give rise to the mind by dwelling nowhere. (Where there is nothing, there is something. (The fifth section, right).
Building upon the preceding statement that "even dharmas should be relinquished," let us proceed further. It is not only views that should be relinquished;
moreover, there are no dharmas at all. From the stage of *srotāpanna* up to the attainment of Buddhahood, all are Buddha-dharmas, and yet none are Buddha-dharmas.
This is because they are all uniformly the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). When the ultimate state of non-existence is reached, it is pure. It is purity.
When this state is reached, there is a profound stillness in which no things exist; yet all principles of the world emerge from this.
This is called "generating the mind by dwelling nowhere. If one dwells anywhere, one will be unable to generate that mind.
Therefore, the essential method for remaining in suchness and simultaneously subduing [the mind] lies in generating the mind while having no place of abiding.
Only then can one attain Buddhahood; only then can one bring all sentient beings to parinirvāṇa.
The great purport of the Buddha’s teaching to Subhūti is, in brief, exhausted here.
"Subhūti, suppose there were a person whose body was like Sumeru, the king of mountains.
What do you think? Would that body be large? Subhūti replied, "It would be very large, World-Honored One. Why is this? The Buddha has taught that it is not a body; it is called a 'great body.

(If one speaks of a body in terms of physical substance, then even the giant Gūnmobā would not suffice to be considered large. A body like Sumeru, the king of mountains, is in fact no-body; therefore, it is called a 'great body. This parable is established to introduce the following [teaching on] non-existence.)"
[The Profound Meaning].
Subhūti, suppose there were as many Ganges Rivers as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River. What do you think?
Would the sands of all those Ganges Rivers be numerous? Subhūti replied, "They would be very numerous, World-Honored One."
"Even all those Ganges Rivers are already countless, let alone their sands. Subhūti, I now tell you the truth:

if there were a son of good family or a daughter of good family who, with the seven treasures, filled as many trichiliocosm worlds as there are grains of sand in those Ganges Rivers and gave them as a gift, would they gain much merit? Subhūti replied:

Fearing that people might mistake blessings for merits and thereby become attached to them, [the text clarifies that] such [attachment] is precisely not non-self.

To have a view of self, person, multitude, or life-span is inherently to possess the view of a self, the view of a person, the view of a sentient being, and the view of a life-span.
